steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our systems paper on GraphMini, which speeds up graph pattern matching using auxiliary graphs. Explain the problem and prior work on set operations, our pruning idea, the research questions it raises, headline results, and a list of contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Graph pattern matching is a basic problem that comes up in many common graph mining tasks and real-world applications, like analyzing social networks and protein-protein interaction networks. It is also the basic building block of several graph mining systems. The problem is hard because the search space and the size of the intermediate data grow exponentially with the size of the data graph and the query graph.

Graph pattern matching needs a large number of set operations on the adjacency lists of the input graph. These set operations are a well-known performance bottleneck, and prior research has focused on speeding them up. State-of-the-art work reduced the number of set operations by caching intermediate results to remove redundant operations and by using better query execution schedules. Other work proposed better implementations of the set operation.

In this paper we explore a different direction to speed up set operations, which is complementary to these: making the adjacency lists that are the input to those operations smaller. Graph pattern matching systems usually match one query vertex or edge at a time, with nested loops. Our basic insight is that when we match a query vertex in a loop, we can already find some data vertices in the data graph that will never be matched in deeper loops. So we can proactively prune these vertices from the adjacency lists and make the lists shorter, which speeds up the set operations on these lists in deeper loops, and the query results do not change. We propose a new data structure, the auxiliary graph, to keep track of pruned adjacency lists on the fly during query execution. We implement this idea in GraphMini, a new single-host graph pattern-matching system that generates query execution code to build, maintain, and reuse auxiliary graphs efficiently.

- Research questions
  - criteria for which lists can be pruned and how, safely
  - multiple auxiliary graphs from same list, each tailored to a query vertex; further online pruning at deeper loops
  - memory overhead only small fraction of data graph
  - pruning not always faster: upfront cost amortized in deeper loops; reuse unknown; always pruning inconsistent
  - cost model from runtime statistics estimates gains before pruning; beats simple heuristics
  - compile-time optimizations: remove runtime checks for picking pruned list version, reuse auxiliary graphs to build others, load balancing across parallel worker threads
- Evaluation
  - up to 30.6x over GraphPi (cite), 60.7x over Dryadic (cite)
  - code generation: minimal impact on end-to-end query time
- Contributions
  - proactive graph pruning via auxiliary graph
  - cost model for amortization
  - GraphMini system with compile-time optimizations
  - experiments: substantially faster than state of the art

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Graph pattern matching is a basic problem that comes up in many common graph mining tasks and real-world applications, like analyzing social networks and protein-protein interaction networks. It is also the basic building block of several graph mining systems. The problem is hard because the search space and the size of the intermediate data grow exponentially with the size of the data graph and the query graph.

Graph pattern matching needs a large number of set operations on the adjacency lists of the input graph. These set operations are a well-known performance bottleneck, and prior research has focused on speeding them up. State-of-the-art work reduced the number of set operations by caching intermediate results to remove redundant operations and by using better query execution schedules. Other work proposed better implementations of the set operation.

In this paper we explore a different direction to speed up set operations, which is complementary to these: making the adjacency lists that are the input to those operations smaller. Graph pattern matching systems usually match one query vertex or edge at a time, with nested loops. Our basic insight is that when we match a query vertex in a loop, we can already find some data vertices in the data graph that will never be matched in deeper loops. So we can proactively prune these vertices from the adjacency lists and make the lists shorter, which speeds up the set operations on these lists in deeper loops, and the query results do not change. We propose a new data structure, the auxiliary graph, to keep track of pruned adjacency lists on the fly during query execution. We implement this idea in GraphMini, a new single-host graph pattern-matching system that generates query execution code to build, maintain, and reuse auxiliary graphs efficiently.

GraphMini deals with several research questions. First, we set criteria for which adjacency lists can be pruned and how to prune them safely, without changing the result of a query. The technique keeps multiple auxiliary graphs from pruning the same adjacency list, and each auxiliary graph is tailored to speed up matching a specific query vertex. These auxiliary graphs can be pruned further online at deeper loops as more intermediate results are available. Our experiments show the memory overhead of storing auxiliary graphs is only a small fraction of the data graph.

Pruning adjacency lists keeps correctness but it does not always speed up computation. Building an auxiliary graph has an upfront cost that needs to be amortized in deeper loops. It is hard to decide if the gains are bigger than the costs, because we cannot know how often an auxiliary graph will be reused later. Always pruning does not give consistent speedups. So we build a cost model that uses runtime statistics to estimate the gains of pruning an adjacency list before it is actually pruned. We show that using the cost model does better than simple heuristics.

GraphMini also implements a set of compile-time optimizations to minimize the computation costs of building, managing, and retrieving auxiliary graphs. These include removing runtime checks for getting the most suitable version of the pruned adjacency lists, reusing auxiliary graphs to build other auxiliary graphs, and techniques to balance load across parallel worker threads.

Our evaluation shows GraphMini is faster than state-of-the-art systems like GraphPi and Dryadic, by up to 30.6x and 60.7x respectively. Also, the code generation algorithm only has a minimal impact on the end-to-end query execution time.

In summary, our contributions are:

- We propose proactive graph pruning using a new data structure called auxiliary graph, to speed up graph pattern matching a lot without changing the query results.

- We propose a cost model to estimate if the cost of pruning an adjacency list will be amortized.

- We implement a new single host graph pattern matching system called GraphMini, which generates query execution code that is tailored to maximize the benefit of proactive pruning, using several compile-time optimizations.

- We show in experiments that GraphMini is substantially faster than state-of-the-art approaches.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Graph pattern matching is a fundamental problem in many common graph mining tasks and real-world applications, such as analyzing social networks [1,2] and protein-protein interaction networks [3]. It is also the basic building block of several graph mining systems [4,5,6,7]. The problem is challenging because the search space and the size of intermediate data increase exponentially with the size of the data graph and the query graph.

Graph pattern matching involves performing a large number of set operations on the adjacency lists of the input graph. These set operations are a well-known performance bottleneck, and speeding them up has been the focus of prior research [8]. State-of-the-art work reduced the number of set operations by caching intermediate results to eliminate redundant operations [5] and by using better query execution schedules [9]. Other work has proposed better implementations of the set operation [8,10,11,12].

This paper explores a different and complementary direction to speed up set operations: reducing the size of the adjacency lists given as input to those operations. Graph pattern matching systems usually match one query vertex or edge at a time, using nested loops. Our basic insight is that, when we match a query vertex in a loop, we can already identify some data vertices that will never be matched in deeper loops. We can thus proactively prune these vertices from adjacency lists to make them shorter, accelerating the set operations on these lists in deeper loops without changing the query results. We propose a new data structure, the auxiliary graph, to keep track of pruned adjacency lists on the fly during query execution. We materialize this idea in GraphMini, a novel single-host graph pattern-matching system that generates query execution code to efficiently build, maintain, and reuse auxiliary graphs.

GraphMini addresses several research questions. First, we establish criteria to identify which adjacency lists can be pruned and how to prune them safely, without changing the result of a query. The technique maintains multiple auxiliary graphs from pruning the same adjacency list, each tailored to speed up the matching of a specific query vertex. These auxiliary graphs can be further pruned online at deeper loops as more intermediate results become available. Our experiments show that the memory overhead of storing auxiliary graphs is only a small fraction of the data graph.

Pruning adjacency lists preserves correctness, but it does not always speed up computation. Building an auxiliary graph entails an upfront cost that must be amortized in deeper loops. Deciding whether the gains outweigh the costs is challenging, because we cannot know how often an auxiliary graph will be reused in the future, and always pruning does not yield consistent speedups. We thus build a cost model that leverages runtime statistics to estimate the gains of pruning an adjacency list before it is actually pruned. We show that the cost model outperforms simple heuristics.

GraphMini also implements a set of compile-time optimizations to minimize the costs of building, managing, and retrieving auxiliary graphs. These include removing runtime checks for retrieving the most suitable version of the pruned adjacency lists, reusing auxiliary graphs to build other auxiliary graphs, and techniques to balance load across parallel worker threads.

Our evaluation shows that GraphMini outperforms state-of-the-art systems like GraphPi [9] and Dryadic [7] by up to 30.6x and 60.7x, respectively. In addition, the code generation algorithm has a minimal impact on end-to-end query execution time.

To summarize, we make the following contributions:

- We propose proactive graph pruning via a new data structure called auxiliary graph, which substantially speeds up graph pattern matching without changing the query results.

- We propose a cost model to estimate whether the cost of pruning an adjacency list will be amortized.

- We implement GraphMini, a novel single host graph pattern matching system that generates query execution code tailored to maximize the benefit of proactive pruning using several compile-time optimizations.

- We experimentally show that GraphMini is substantially faster than state-of-the-art approaches.
